lessons.title: Android Development with Kotlin: Setup and Your First App
lessons.metaTitle: Android with Kotlin: Setup and First App
lessons.description: Install Android Studio, learn the project structure and Gradle, and run your first Kotlin and Jetpack Compose app on an emulator or phone.

content.text: Android is the operating system on most of the phones in the world. An Android developer builds the apps on those phones: banking, delivery, maps, learning, health, games. Companies hire Android developers to build and maintain these apps, and small teams and freelancers build their own products too. The good news for a learner is that you can start on almost any computer. Android Studio runs on Windows, macOS and Linux, and every tool you need is free.

Modern Android work uses three main ideas, and you will meet all of them in this course. **Kotlin** is the programming language Google recommends for Android. It is short, readable and safe. **Jetpack Compose** is the modern toolkit for building screens: you write functions that describe the screen, and Android draws it. **Android Studio** is the program where you write, build and test the app. Older apps use Java and XML layout files, and you will still see them at work, but new apps are written in Kotlin with Compose, so that is what we teach.
What you will build in this course

This is a hands-on course. After two lessons that teach the Kotlin language, you build ten complete applications, each one a little harder than the last, and each one teaches one group of skills that real teams use.

items: **Tip calculator**: screens, state and input.
**To-do list**: lists, ViewModel and state hoisting.
**Unit converter**: forms, menus and validation.
**Quiz app**: several screens with navigation.
**Notes app**: a database on the phone with Room.
**Weather app**: loading data from the internet with Retrofit and coroutines.
**Expense tracker**: money, Flow and totals from a database.
**Posts reader**: images, search, pull to refresh and a detail screen.
**Habit tracker**: saved settings with DataStore and a daily reminder with WorkManager.
**Recipe book**: a capstone with Hilt, Retrofit, Room and bottom navigation.

content.text: The last two lessons cover testing and releasing an app to the Google Play Store. Everything is in plain English, and every project lists its files, its steps and what you should see on screen.

The code in this course was syntax-checked with a Kotlin parser. It was not compiled or run on a device while the course was written, so type it in, build it in Android Studio and fix any small differences your tool versions show. Library versions move quickly: when Android Studio suggests a newer version of a library, accept it and read the release notes if something stops compiling.
Install Android Studio

items: Go to the official Android developer website, search for Android Studio and download the version for your system. It is free.
Run the installer and accept the standard setup. It downloads the Android SDK, the tools that build apps, and may take a while.
Open Android Studio. On first start it offers to install more components. Let it finish.

Check that your computer has enough free disk space and memory. Emulators are heavy, and a computer with 8 GB of memory is the practical minimum. If yours is slow, you can run your app on a real Android phone instead (the next section shows how).

content.text: Create your first project

items: Choose **New Project** and pick the **Empty Activity** template. This template uses Kotlin and Jetpack Compose.
Name it `Hello`. Keep the package name suggested, such as `com.example.hello`. The package name is the unique ID of your app.

Choose a Minimum SDK. API 26 or higher is a sensible choice today, because it covers nearly all active phones while giving you modern features. Android Studio shows the percentage of devices each choice covers.
Click Finish and wait. The first **Gradle sync** downloads libraries and can take several minutes. The bottom bar shows progress.

content.text: Gradle is the build tool. It reads the build files, downloads the libraries you ask for and turns your code into an installable app file called an APK or an AAB. You will edit one file often: `app/build.gradle.kts`, where you add libraries in a block called `dependencies`.
The project structure
Android Studio shows many folders. These are the ones that matter now.

Hello/
  app/
    build.gradle.kts            libraries and app settings (you edit this)
    src/main/
      AndroidManifest.xml       the app's ID card: name, icon, screens, permissions
      java/com/example/hello/
        MainActivity.kt         the first screen that opens
        ui/theme/               colours, fonts and the app theme
      res/                      images, icons, strings
  build.gradle.kts              settings shared by all modules
  gradle/libs.versions.toml     one list of library versions
Open `MainActivity.kt`. It contains code like the one below. Names may differ slightly between Android Studio versions, and that is fine.

An **Activity** is one screen of the app, and `onCreate` runs when it opens. `setContent` says: draw this with Compose. `Greeting` is a **composable function**, marked with `@Composable`. It does not return anything. It describes a piece of screen, here one line of text. That single idea, small functions that describe the screen, is the whole of Compose.
Run it

items: Open **Device Manager** in Android Studio and create a virtual device, for example a recent Pixel phone. Download the system image when asked.
Choose the device at the top of the window and press the green **Run** button.
The emulator starts, which can take a minute the first time. Then your app opens and shows the greeting.

content.text: To use a real phone instead, open Settings, tap the build number seven times to unlock Developer options, turn on USB debugging, connect the phone with a cable and allow the computer. The phone then appears in the device list.

Now make a change. Edit the text to say `Hello, my first app!` and run again. Add a second `Text` line below the first one. If both appear on the same line or overlap, that is a first lesson in layout: you will fix it in lesson 4 with a `Column`. This loop of change, run, look is how you will learn the rest of the course.
Your task

items: Install Android Studio and create a project from the Empty Activity template named Hello.
Run it on an emulator or a real phone and see the greeting.
Change the greeting text to your own name and run it again.
Open `AndroidManifest.xml` and find the app name and the line that marks `MainActivity` as the screen that opens first.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The emulator or phone shows your changed text.
Gradle finishes the sync with no red errors.
You can say in one sentence what an Activity, a composable and Gradle are.

steps.say: You write Kotlin code and Compose functions in files such as MainActivity.kt.
Gradle compiles the code and bundles it with images and settings.
The result is an APK file, an installable Android app.
Android Studio installs it on the emulator or your phone and starts it.

faqs.q: Do I need a powerful computer?
faqs.a: A computer with 8 GB of memory works, but emulators can be slow. If yours struggles, plug in a real Android phone with USB debugging turned on and run your apps there.

faqs.q: Should I learn Java or Kotlin for Android?
faqs.a: Kotlin. Google recommends it for new Android work, and most new tutorials and apps use it. You may meet Java in older code at work, and it is easy to read once you know Kotlin.

faqs.q: Is Jetpack Compose better than XML layouts?
faqs.a: For new apps, yes: it needs less code and updates the screen from your data. Many existing apps still use XML views, so learn Compose first and the old views later when a job needs them.

lessons.title: Kotlin Basics: Variables, Types, Functions and Control Flow
lessons.description: Learn core Kotlin: val and var, types, string templates, if and when, loops, and functions with default and named arguments, with runnable samples.

content.text: Before you build screens, you need to read and write Kotlin comfortably. This lesson covers the parts of the language you will use in every app. Each example is a tiny program with a `main` function. To run them without making a whole Android project, open the free Kotlin Playground on the official Kotlin website, paste the code and press Run. You can also create a new Kotlin file in Android Studio and run its `main` function.
Values and variables

Kotlin has two keywords for storing data. `val` makes a value that cannot be reassigned after it is set. `var` makes a variable that can change. Prefer `val`: code is easier to reason about when most things never change. Kotlin works out the type from the value (this is called type inference), so you rarely write the type, but you can.

fun main() {
    val name = "Asha"          // val: cannot be reassigned
    var steps = 4200           // var: can change
    steps += 800

    val goal: Int = 10_000     // the type can be written out
    val ratio = steps.toDouble() / goal
    val percent = (ratio * 100).toInt()

    println("$name walked $steps steps")
    println("That is $percent% of the goal")
    println("Steps left: ${goal - steps}")
}
The `$name` and `${goal - steps}` parts are **string templates**: Kotlin puts the value into the text. Use `$name` for a simple name and `${ ... }` for any expression. Expected output:

Asha walked 5000 steps
That is 50% of the goal
Steps left: 5000

Common types are `Int` (whole numbers), `Double` (numbers with decimals), `Boolean` (true or false), `String` (text) and `Char` (one character). Kotlin does not change types silently. You cannot add an `Int` to a `Double` without a conversion such as `toDouble()`. That strictness stops a whole group of bugs.
Decisions and loops

`if` works as you expect, and in Kotlin it is also an **expression**, which means it gives back a value. `when` is like a more readable chain of `if` and `else if`. Loops use `for` with a range such as `1..3`, and `while`.

Round 1
Round 2
Round 3
3 2 1 Go!
82 is a pass, grade B
Functions

A function is a named piece of code that you can call many times. It lists its inputs (parameters) and its output type after a colon. A function whose body is a single expression can be written with `=`. You can give parameters **default values** and call them with **named arguments**, which makes calls easy to read. `vararg` lets a function take any number of values.

fun greet(name: String, greeting: String = "Hello"): String = "$greeting, $name!"

fun average(vararg numbers: Int): Double =
    if (numbers.isEmpty()) 0.0 else numbers.sum().toDouble() / numbers.size

fun main() {
    println(greet("Ravi"))
    println(greet("Ravi", greeting = "Welcome"))
    println(average(70, 80, 90))
    println(average())
}

Hello, Ravi!
Welcome, Ravi!
80.0
0.0
Compose uses these two features all the time. A call such as `Text(text = "Hi", fontSize = 20.sp)` is a function with named arguments, and most of its parameters have defaults.
Why this matters for Android

Every Android screen you build uses these basics. State is stored in `val` and `var`. Buttons run functions. Lists of data are looped over. A `when` decides which screen part to show. If a later lesson feels hard, the cause is nearly always a gap here, so come back and rerun these samples.
Your task

items: Run all three samples in the Kotlin Playground and compare each output with the lesson.
Change `Variables.kt` so the goal is 8,000 steps and the person walked 6,500. Check that the percent and steps left are right.
Write a function `isEven(n: Int): Boolean` and use it inside a `for` loop that prints the even numbers from 1 to 10.
Add a `when` to `Control.kt` that prints a different message for a score of exactly 100.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Your outputs match the expected text for each sample.
You can say the difference between `val` and `var`.
You can explain what a string template is and write one.

steps.say: val stores a value that never changes. Prefer it.
var stores a value you are allowed to change later.
A function takes values in and works on them.
It gives back a result, which your program prints or shows on screen.

faqs.q: Why does Kotlin prefer val over var?
faqs.a: A value that never changes cannot be changed by mistake somewhere else in the program. That makes bugs easier to find. Use var only when the value really has to change.

faqs.q: Do I need to write types everywhere?
faqs.a: No. Kotlin works out the type from the value. You write a type when it is not obvious, for function parameters (always) and for public APIs.

faqs.q: Where can I run Kotlin without Android Studio?
faqs.a: The Kotlin Playground on the official Kotlin website runs small programs in your browser. Android Studio can also run a `main` function from any Kotlin file.

options: val cannot be reassigned, var can

quiz.q: What does "Total: ${a + b}" do?
options: Puts the result of a + b into the text

quiz.q: What are named arguments for?
options: Making calls easy to read, e.g. greet(name = "Ravi")

lessons.title: Kotlin Classes, Collections, Null Safety and Lambdas
lessons.metaTitle: Kotlin Classes, Collections and Null Safety
lessons.description: Learn data classes, interfaces, list helpers like filter and map, null safety with ?. and ?:, and lambdas: the Kotlin skills every Android app uses.

content.text: This lesson covers the second half of the Kotlin you need. It is the part that makes Kotlin feel different from older languages: classes that take one line, collections you can transform with short code, and a type system that prevents the most common crash in programming, the null pointer error.
Classes and data classes

A class describes a kind of thing: a user, a product, a note. A **data class** is a class whose main job is to hold data. Kotlin writes `toString`, `equals` and a `copy` function for you. In Android you will write dozens of data classes: one for each row in a database and each item in a list. Regular classes can **inherit** from another class (mark the parent `open`) and **implement interfaces**, which are lists of functions a class promises to have.

Product(name=Pen, price=1.5, stock=20)
Product(name=Pen, price=1.2, stock=20)
Meera has 150.0 (interest rate 4.0%)
13.0

Notice `private set` on `balance`. Anyone can read the balance, but only the class can change it, so the rule "a deposit must be positive" cannot be bypassed. Hiding what outsiders should not touch is the heart of good class design, and you will use it again in ViewModels.
Collections

Lists, sets and maps hold groups of values. `listOf` makes a list that cannot change, and `mutableListOf` makes one that can. The real power is in the helper functions: `filter` keeps some items, `map` turns every item into something else, `sortedBy` orders them, `groupBy` sorts them into buckets, and `sumOf` or `average` fold them into one number. Each takes a **lambda**, a small block of code in braces. Inside the lambda `it` means the current item.

data class Student(val name: String, val marks: Int)

fun main() {
    val students = listOf(Student("Asha", 82), Student("Ben", 45), Student("Chen", 91), Student("Dev", 67))

    val passed = students.filter { it.marks >= 50 }          // keep some items
    val names = passed.map { it.name }                        // change each item
    val best = students.maxByOrNull { it.marks }              // find one
    val average = students.map { it.marks }.average()         // fold into one value

    println(names)
    println(best?.name)
    println(average)
    println(students.sortedByDescending { it.marks }.map { it.name })

    val byResult = students.groupBy { if (it.marks >= 50) "pass" else "fail" }
    println(byResult.mapValues { (_, list) -> list.size })

    val mutable = mutableListOf("a", "b")
    mutable.add("c")
    println(mutable)
}

[Asha, Chen, Dev]
Chen
71.25
[Chen, Asha, Dev, Ben]
{pass=3, fail=1}
[a, b, c]
Null safety

In many languages any value may secretly be null, and using it crashes the app. In Kotlin a normal type such as `String` can never be null. A type that can be null is written with a question mark, `String?`, and the compiler forces you to deal with it. The safe-call operator `?.` stops quietly when the value is null, and the Elvis operator `?:` supplies a default. `let` runs a block only when the value is not null. Avoid `!!`, which means "crash if this is null".

fun lengthOf(text: String?): Int = text?.length ?: 0      // ?. stops at null, ?: gives a default

fun main() {
    var nickname: String? = null
    println(nickname?.uppercase())          // null, no crash
    println(lengthOf(nickname))             // 0

    nickname = "kit"
    println(lengthOf(nickname))             // 3

    nickname?.let { println("Nickname is $it") }   // runs only when not null

    val input = "12a"
    val number = input.toIntOrNull()        // null instead of an exception
    println(number ?: "not a number")
}

null
0
3
Nickname is kit
not a number
Lambdas and functions as values

A function can be passed around like any other value. A function that takes another function is called a higher-order function. When the last parameter is a function you may write the lambda after the brackets, which is called a trailing lambda. Compose depends on this: `Button(onClick = { ... }) { Text("Go") }` passes one lambda for the click and a trailing lambda for the content.

Run number 1
Run number 2
Run number 3
42
[Kotlin, Android, Compose]
kotlin | android | compose
These outputs were worked out by hand from the code. Run each sample in the Kotlin Playground to confirm them, and tell us if any line differs.
Your task

items: Create a `data class Book(val title: String, val pages: Int)` and a list of four books.
Print the titles of books with more than 200 pages, using `filter` and `map`.
Print the average page count and the title of the longest book. Use `?.` so the code is safe if the list is empty.
Write a function `describe(text: String?): String` that returns "empty" when the text is null or blank and the text in capitals otherwise.

items: Your list code prints the right titles and average.
You can explain what `String?` means and why `!!` is risky.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a class and a data class?
faqs.a: A data class is a class meant to hold data. Kotlin generates toString, equals, hashCode and copy for it. Use it for things like rows and list items.

faqs.q: Why is null safety such a big deal?
faqs.a: Null pointer errors are one of the most common crashes in apps. Kotlin makes nullability part of the type, so the compiler warns you before the app ever runs.

faqs.q: What does `it` mean in a lambda?
faqs.a: When a lambda has exactly one input, Kotlin names it `it` automatically. You can write your own name instead, such as `student ->`, when that reads better.

lessons.title: Jetpack Compose Basics and Project 1: Tip Calculator
lessons.description: Learn composable functions, Column, Row, modifiers, state and recomposition, then build a complete tip calculator app with a slider, a switch and a bill split.

content.text: You now know enough Kotlin to build screens. In **Jetpack Compose** a screen is a function that describes what should be visible for the current data. When the data changes, Compose runs the function again and updates only what changed. This idea has a name, **recomposition**, and it replaces the old way of finding views and changing them by hand.
The pieces of a Compose screen

items: **Composable functions** are marked `@Composable`. They can call other composables.
**Layouts** place things: `Column` stacks vertically, `Row` lines up horizontally, `Box` stacks on top of each other, and `LazyColumn` shows long lists efficiently.
**Widgets** are things the user sees and uses: `Text`, `Button`, `OutlinedTextField`, `Slider`, `Switch`, `Card`, `Checkbox`.
**Modifiers** change how a composable looks and behaves: `Modifier.padding(16.dp).fillMaxWidth()`. The order matters, because each modifier wraps the result of the one before it.
**Material 3** gives you ready-made, good-looking widgets and a theme with colours and text styles.

content.text: State: the most important idea

State is data that can change and that the screen depends on, such as the text in a box or whether a switch is on. In Compose you keep state in a `MutableState` and read its value in the function. When the value changes, Compose reads it again and redraws. You make state with `remember { mutableStateOf(...) }`. The `remember` part keeps the value between redraws. Without it the value would reset to its start every time the function ran.

Each tap raises `count`. Compose notices the change, runs `Counter` again, and the button shows the new text. The `by` keyword lets you use `count` like a normal variable. Use `mutableIntStateOf`, `mutableFloatStateOf` and `mutableStateOf` depending on the type.
Project 1: Tip Calculator

The user types a bill, chooses a tip with a slider, picks how many people share it and sees the totals. It teaches state, text input with a number keyboard, a slider, a switch and a card. All the arithmetic lives in a plain Kotlin function, which keeps it separate from the screen and, in lesson 14, easy to test.

Add three files next to `MainActivity.kt`: `TipMath.kt` and `TipScreen.kt`. Replace the contents of `MainActivity.kt` as shown below.
No extra libraries are needed for this project.

TipCalc/app/src/main/java/com/example/tipcalc/

  TipScreen.kt       the screen: input, slider, switch, results
  TipMath.kt         the calculation, with no Android code in it
The code
**`app/src/main/java/com/example/tipcalc/MainActivity.kt`**
`enableEdgeToEdge()` lets the app draw behind the system bars, and `systemBarsPadding()` later keeps text out from under them. `Surface` gives a background colour from the theme.
**`app/src/main/java/com/example/tipcalc/TipMath.kt`**
`require` checks the input and throws a clear error if it is wrong. Because this function is plain Kotlin you can run it with no phone at all.
**`app/src/main/java/com/example/tipcalc/TipScreen.kt`**
How it works

items: Four pieces of state live at the top of `TipScreen`: the bill text, tip percent, number of people and the round-up switch.
The bill is kept as text, because the user types it. `toDoubleOrNull()` turns it into a number, or null if the box is empty or not a number, and `?: 0.0` makes that zero.
The result is recalculated on every recomposition. That is cheap here, and it means the totals can never be out of date.
`Modifier.weight(1f)` makes the label take all spare width so the buttons sit on the right.

content.text: Expected output

The screen shows the title, a bill box, a slider at 15%, a people row set to 1, a round-up switch and a card. Type 100 as the bill: the card shows Tip 15.00, Total 115.00 and Each person pays 115.00. Press + twice for three people: each person pays 38.33. Turn on rounding with a bill of 33 and 15%: the tip changes from 4.95 to 5.00.

Add a row of three buttons (10%, 15%, 20%) that set the tip percent in one tap.

The event changes a value in state.
Compose sees the change and runs the composable function again.
The function describes the new screen and Compose draws only what changed.

faqs.q: What is recomposition?
faqs.a: Recomposition is Compose running a composable function again because some state it reads has changed. It updates only the parts of the screen that are affected.

faqs.q: Why do I need remember?
faqs.a: Without remember the value would reset every time the function runs again. remember keeps it for as long as the composable stays on screen.

faqs.q: What is the difference between remember and rememberSaveable?
faqs.a: remember loses its value when the phone rotates or the process is recreated. rememberSaveable also saves the value, so it survives those changes. Use it for things the user typed.

quiz.q: What is recomposition?
options: Compose running a composable again because its state changed

quiz.q: Why is remember needed with mutableStateOf?
options: It keeps the value between recompositions

lessons.title: Project 2: To-Do List with ViewModel and LazyColumn
lessons.description: Build a to-do list app in Compose and learn ViewModel, StateFlow, LazyColumn with keys, state hoisting and unidirectional data flow with complete, working code.

content.text: In the tip calculator, all the state lived inside one composable. That is fine for a small screen, but real apps have rules and data that must survive screen rotation and be shared between screens. The standard answer in Android is the **ViewModel**. A ViewModel is a class that holds the state of a screen and the logic that changes it. It lives longer than the composable, so it survives rotation. This project builds a to-do list and teaches the pattern you will use in every remaining project.
Concepts in this project

items: **ViewModel**: holds screen state and logic, and survives rotation.
**StateFlow**: a stream that always holds a current value. The ViewModel changes it and the screen watches it.
**collectAsStateWithLifecycle**: turns a StateFlow into Compose state, and stops collecting when the app is in the background.
**State hoisting**: a composable does not own its data. It receives the value and the events (lambdas) from above. This makes small composables simple and reusable.
**Unidirectional data flow**: events go up, state comes down. The UI asks the ViewModel to change something, the ViewModel updates the state, and the UI redraws from the new state.
**LazyColumn**: shows only the rows that are visible, so a list of thousands stays fast. Give each item a stable `key` so Compose can move and animate rows correctly.

content.text: Create the project

items: Create an Empty Activity project named `Todo`, package `com.example.todo`.
Open `app/build.gradle.kts` and add these lines to `dependencies`, then press Sync Now.
Add the four Kotlin files shown below.

content.text: **`app/build.gradle.kts (dependencies)`**

Todo/app/src/main/java/com/example/todo/
  MainActivity.kt     shows TodoScreen
  Task.kt             the data: id, title, done
  TodoViewModel.kt    the list and the rules (add, toggle, remove)
  TodoScreen.kt       the UI that shows the list and sends events
The code
**`app/src/main/java/com/example/todo/Task.kt`**

package com.example.todo

data class Task(
    val id: Long,
    val title: String,
    val done: Boolean = false
)
**`app/src/main/java/com/example/todo/TodoViewModel.kt`**

Read `TodoViewModel` carefully. `_tasks` is private and mutable: only the ViewModel can change it. `tasks` is the public, read-only view of it. Each function builds a new list with `update` instead of changing the old list. Because the list is never edited in place, Compose can tell that something changed. This "copy, do not mutate" habit prevents many bugs.
**`app/src/main/java/com/example/todo/TodoScreen.kt`**

`TodoScreen` collects the state and passes small pieces down. `TaskRow` knows nothing about the ViewModel: it gets one `Task` and two lambdas, `onToggle` and `onDelete`. That is state hoisting. A composable like this is easy to preview and test.
**`app/src/main/java/com/example/todo/MainActivity.kt`**
Expected output

The first screen shows the title To-Do, a text box with a plus button, the line "0 left, 0 done" and the message "Nothing to do. Add your first task above." Add Buy milk and Call Dad: both appear and the line reads "2 left, 0 done". Tick Buy milk: its text gets a line through it and the line reads "1 left, 1 done". Rotate the phone: the list stays, because the ViewModel survived. Press Clear finished tasks and only Call Dad remains.
This list lives in memory only. If you close the app completely, the tasks are gone. You will fix that in project 5 with a real database.

lessons.title: Project 3: Unit Converter with Dropdown Menus
lessons.description: Build an Android unit converter in Compose with dropdown menus, length, weight and temperature categories, validation and clean Kotlin logic.

content.text: The unit converter is a small app with a clear job: turn 5 kilometres into miles, or 100 degrees Celsius into Fahrenheit. It is useful for learning because it forces you to think about data design. How do you store dozens of units without writing a huge `if` chain? The answer is a table of data, and it is a lesson you will reuse in every later project: when you feel yourself copying code, describe the differences as data instead.
Concepts in this project

items: **Data-driven design**: each unit is a small object with two functions, `toBase` and `fromBase`. To convert A to B, change A to the base unit, then change the base unit to B. With N units you write N pairs of formulas, not N times N.
**Dropdown menus**: `ExposedDropdownMenuBox` or a `DropdownMenu` anchored to a button, with items that call a lambda when chosen.
**Validation**: the input is text, so it may be empty or invalid. The code must show a clear message and never crash.
**Pure functions**: the conversion has no Android code, so you can test it with no phone.

content.text: Create the project

items: New Empty Activity project `Converter`, package `com.example.converter`. No extra libraries are needed.
Add `Units.kt` and `ConverterScreen.kt`, and replace `MainActivity.kt`.

content.text:
Converter/app/src/main/java/com/example/converter/
  MainActivity.kt      shows ConverterScreen
  Units.kt             unit definitions and the convert function
  ConverterScreen.kt   input, two pickers, result
The code
**`app/src/main/java/com/example/converter/Units.kt`**

package com.example.converter

/** Every unit knows how to turn itself into a base unit and back. */
data class UnitDef(val name: String, val toBase: (Double) -> Double, val fromBase: (Double) -> Double)

data class Category(val name: String, val units: List<UnitDef>)

private fun linear(name: String, factor: Double) = UnitDef(name, { it * factor }, { it / factor })

val categories = listOf(
    Category(
        "Length (base: metre)",
        listOf(linear("Metre", 1.0), linear("Kilometre", 1000.0), linear("Centimetre", 0.01),
            linear("Mile", 1609.344), linear("Foot", 0.3048), linear("Inch", 0.0254))
    ),
    Category(
        "Weight (base: kilogram)",
        listOf(linear("Kilogram", 1.0), linear("Gram", 0.001), linear("Pound", 0.45359237), linear("Ounce", 0.028349523125))
    ),
    Category(
        "Temperature (base: Celsius)",
        listOf(
            UnitDef("Celsius", { it }, { it }),
            UnitDef("Fahrenheit", { (it - 32) * 5 / 9 }, { it * 9 / 5 + 32 }),
            UnitDef("Kelvin", { it - 273.15 }, { it + 273.15 })
        )
    )
)

fun convert(value: Double, from: UnitDef, to: UnitDef): Double = to.fromBase(from.toBase(value))

Look at temperature. Celsius is the base unit, so `toBase` for Fahrenheit is `(f - 32) * 5 / 9` and `fromBase` is `c * 9 / 5 + 32`. Length and weight units just multiply by a factor. Because every unit follows the same shape, the screen needs no special cases at all.
**`app/src/main/java/com/example/converter/ConverterScreen.kt`**
**`app/src/main/java/com/example/converter/MainActivity.kt`**
How it works

items: The category chips choose a list of units. When the category changes, both pickers are reset to sensible units from the new list.

`Picker` is a reusable composable: it shows the current unit, opens a menu when tapped and reports the choice through `onPick`. Its own `expanded` state is local, because nobody else cares whether a menu is open.
The result is recomputed from the typed text. If the text is not a number, no result is shown instead of an error.

content.text: Expected output

Choose Length, type 5, from Kilometres to Miles: the result reads about 3.107. Choose Temperature, type 100, from Celsius to Fahrenheit: 212. Type 0 from Celsius to Fahrenheit: 32. Type 72 from Fahrenheit to Celsius: about 22.22. Swapping the two units gives the reverse conversion.

toBase turns kilometres into metres: 5000.
fromBase turns metres into miles using the miles factor.
The screen shows the number, about 3.107.

faqs.q: Why convert through a base unit?
faqs.a: It needs only two formulas per unit. Converting directly between every pair of units would need a formula for each pair, which grows very fast.

faqs.q: How do I keep the menu state?
faqs.a: Keep it local with remember when only that composable needs it. Lift it up only if another part of the screen must read or control it.

faqs.q: Is Double accurate enough for money?
faqs.a: No. Double is fine for measurements, but money should be stored as whole cents in a Long or in BigDecimal. Project 7 does exactly that.

options: It needs only two formulas per unit instead of one for each pair

options: Show nothing or a message, never crash

quiz.q: Where should the menu open/closed flag live?
options: In local remember state of the picker

content.text: Almost every real app has more than one screen. A shopping app has a list, a product page, a cart and a checkout. In Compose you do not create many Activities for this. You keep one Activity and use **Navigation Compose**, a library that swaps which composable is shown and keeps a back stack, so the system Back button works as users expect.
Concepts in this project

items: **NavController**: remembers where you are and moves between screens.
**NavHost**: the place on screen where the current destination is drawn. It lists all the routes.
**Routes with arguments**: a route such as `result/{score}/{total}` carries values to the next screen.
**rememberSaveable**: keeps the quiz position through rotation.
**Back stack**: after the result screen you pop back to home so Back does not return to the last question.

lessons.title: Project 5: Notes App with a Room Database
lessons.metaTitle: Project 5: Notes App with Room Database
lessons.description: Build a notes app that saves data on the phone with Room: entity, DAO, Flow and a searchable ViewModel, with add, edit and delete in Compose.

content.text: So far every app forgot its data when closed. Real apps need to store information on the device. Android has SQLite built in, a small database in a file, and the **Room** library makes it pleasant to use from Kotlin. You describe your table as a class, write queries as functions, and Room generates all the boring code and checks your SQL when the app is built.
Concepts in this project

items: **Entity**: a data class marked `@Entity`. One class is one table and one object is one row.
**DAO** (data access object): an interface with functions marked `@Query`, `@Upsert` and `@Delete`. You write the SQL, Room writes the code.
**Database**: an abstract class marked `@Database` that lists the entities and gives you the DAOs.
**Flow**: a DAO function that returns `Flow<List<Note>>` emits a new list every time the table changes. The screen updates by itself, with no refresh code.
**KSP**: a build tool that Room uses to generate its code. You add it as a plugin.

faqs.q: Why does Room use Flow?
faqs.a: A Flow query keeps watching the table. Whenever a row changes it sends the new result, so the screen stays up to date without any manual refresh.

faqs.q: What is a migration?

faqs.q: Can I run Room queries on the main thread?
faqs.a: Not by default, and you should not. Suspend functions and Flow queries run on a background thread for you.

lessons.title: Project 6: Weather App with Retrofit and Coroutines
lessons.description: Build a weather app that loads live data from a free API with Retrofit, kotlinx serialization and coroutines, with loading, success and error states in Compose.

content.text: Most apps talk to a server. Weather, maps, shopping, banking and chat all load data from the internet. Doing this well on a phone is harder than it sounds: the network is slow, it fails, and the app must stay smooth while it waits. In Android you solve this with three tools. **Retrofit** turns a web API into a Kotlin interface. **kotlinx.serialization** turns JSON into Kotlin objects. **Coroutines** let you wait for the network without freezing the screen.
Concepts in this project

items: **REST API and JSON**: you send an HTTP request to a URL and get back text in JSON form.
**Retrofit**: you declare `@GET("forecast") suspend fun ...` and it builds the HTTP call.
**Coroutines and `suspend`**: a suspend function can pause without blocking a thread. `viewModelScope.launch` starts one that is cancelled when the ViewModel goes away.
**UI state**: a sealed class with Loading, Success and Error. The screen shows one of the three, so every case is handled.
**Repository**: a class between the ViewModel and the network, which hides where data comes from.
**Permission**: the app needs `INTERNET` in the manifest.

content.text: This project uses **Open-Meteo**, a free weather API that needs no key, plus its free geocoding endpoint to turn a city name into coordinates. Check its current terms and URL on its website, because public APIs can change.

content.text: An expense tracker looks simple, but it teaches two things that matter in every serious app: how to handle money correctly and how to get answers from a database instead of from loops in your code. You will use Room again, now with sums and groups.
Concepts in this project

items: **Money as whole cents**: `0.1 + 0.2` is not exactly `0.3` in floating-point numbers. Store money as an integer number of cents in a `Long`, and only format it as dollars or rupees for display.
**SQL aggregates**: `SUM(amountCents)` and `GROUP BY category` let the database do the totals quickly.
**Flow for totals**: the total is a Flow too, so it updates the moment you add or remove an expense.
**Flow rows and chips**: `FilterChip` lets the user pick a category, and `FlowRow` wraps the chips onto several lines.
**Reuse**: this project follows the same layers as project 5, so you can see the pattern settle: entity, DAO, database, ViewModel, screen.

lessons.description: Build a habit tracker with streaks saved in Jetpack DataStore and a daily reminder using WorkManager and a notification, including the notification permission.

content.text: Habit trackers show the features that make an app feel alive: it remembers your settings, it keeps a streak and it reminds you at the right time even when closed. This project covers three tools: **DataStore** for small saved data, **WorkManager** for background work, and **notifications** with the permission needed on newer Android versions.
Concepts in this project

items: **DataStore**: the modern replacement for SharedPreferences. It stores small data asynchronously and exposes it as a Flow. This project stores the habit list as JSON text in one key.
**Streak logic**: a pure function counts consecutive days ending today (or yesterday) from a set of completed dates.
**WorkManager**: runs work that must happen even if the app is closed or the phone restarts. A periodic request is not exact, which suits reminders.
**Notification channel**: from Android 8 every notification belongs to a channel the user can control.
**Runtime permission**: from Android 13 the app must ask for `POST_NOTIFICATIONS`. Use the activity result API from Compose, and handle a refusal gracefully.

content.text: The last project joins everything. It searches recipes online, shows details, lets you save favourites that work offline and has a bottom navigation bar. It also introduces **dependency injection** with Hilt, the standard tool for wiring a larger app together, so the code stays organised as it grows.
Concepts in this project

items: **Layers**: UI (screens), ViewModels (state and logic), repository (one place for data), and data sources (Retrofit for the network, Room for the database).
**Dependency injection**: instead of a class creating the things it needs, they are handed in. Hilt creates and shares one Retrofit, one database and one repository for the whole app.
**`@HiltViewModel` and `hiltViewModel()`**: ViewModels get their dependencies automatically.
**SavedStateHandle**: gives the ViewModel the navigation arguments, such as the recipe ID.
**Bottom navigation**: `NavigationBar` switches between Search and Favourites while keeping each screen's state.
**Data source**: TheMealDB, a free recipe API with a public test key. Check its current terms and whether the test key still works before building.

package com.example.recipes

import androidx.room.Entity
import androidx.room.PrimaryKey
import kotlinx.serialization.Serializable
import kotlinx.serialization.json.JsonObject
import kotlinx.serialization.json.contentOrNull
import kotlinx.serialization.json.jsonPrimitive

// What the API sends. TheMealDB uses strIngredient1..strIngredient20, so we read each meal as a JsonObject.
@Serializable
data class MealsResponse(val meals: List<JsonObject>? = null)

// What the app uses everywhere else.
data class Recipe(
    val id: String,
    val name: String,
    val thumb: String,
    val category: String,
    val area: String,
    val instructions: String,
    val ingredients: List<String>
)

private fun JsonObject.str(key: String): String? = this[key]?.jsonPrimitive?.contentOrNull?.trim()?.takeIf { it.isNotEmpty() }

fun JsonObject.toRecipe(): Recipe = Recipe(
    id = str("idMeal") ?: "",
    name = str("strMeal") ?: "Unnamed recipe",
    thumb = str("strMealThumb") ?: "",
    category = str("strCategory") ?: "",
    area = str("strArea") ?: "",
    instructions = str("strInstructions") ?: "",
    ingredients = (1..20).mapNotNull { i ->
        val ingredient = str("strIngredient$i") ?: return@mapNotNull null
        listOfNotNull(str("strMeasure$i"), ingredient).joinToString(" ")
    }
)

// A small copy of a recipe, saved on the phone when the user taps the heart.
@Entity(tableName = "favourites")
data class Favourite(@PrimaryKey val id: String, val name: String, val thumb: String, val category: String)

The API returns each ingredient as separate numbered fields (`strIngredient1`, `strIngredient2`...). The mapper reads the JSON as a generic object and collects the non-empty ones into a clean list, so the rest of the app sees a tidy `Recipe`. This is a common job at the edge of an app: shield your code from messy outside data.

package com.example.recipes

import android.content.Context
import androidx.room.Room
import dagger.Module
import dagger.Provides
import dagger.hilt.InstallIn
import dagger.hilt.android.qualifiers.ApplicationContext
import dagger.hilt.components.SingletonComponent
import kotlinx.serialization.json.Json
import okhttp3.MediaType.Companion.toMediaType
import retrofit2.Retrofit
import retrofit2.converter.kotlinx.serialization.asConverterFactory
import javax.inject.Singleton

// A module tells Hilt how to build things it cannot build by itself (Retrofit, Room).
@Module
@InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
object AppModule {
    @Provides @Singleton
    fun mealApi(): MealApi = Retrofit.Builder()
        .baseUrl("https://www.themealdb.com/api/json/v1/1/")
        .addConverterFactory(Json { ignoreUnknownKeys = true }.asConverterFactory("application/json".toMediaType()))
        .build()
        .create(MealApi::class.java)

    @Provides @Singleton
    fun database(@ApplicationContext context: Context): AppDb =
        Room.databaseBuilder(context, AppDb::class.java, "recipes.db").build()

    @Provides
    fun favouriteDao(db: AppDb): FavouriteDao = db.favouriteDao()
}

lessons.title: Testing and Performance for Android Apps
lessons.metaTitle: Testing and Performance for Android Apps
lessons.description: Learn Android testing: local unit tests, ViewModel tests with coroutines and Compose UI tests, plus tips to keep your app fast and crash-free.

content.text: Apps that work on your phone can still fail on other phones. Tests are small programs that check your code for you, every time, in seconds. They let you change code without fear, and teams expect them. Android has two main kinds.
Two kinds of tests

items: **Local unit tests** live in `src/test` and run on your computer's JVM with no phone. They are fast. Use them for pure functions and ViewModels.
**Instrumented tests** live in `src/androidTest` and run on a device or emulator. They are slower. Use them for Compose UI and for anything that needs Android itself.

content.text: Add the testing libraries to Gradle first.
**`Gradle additions for tests`**

testImplementation("junit:junit:4.13.2")
testImplementation("org.jetbrains.kotlinx:kotlinx-coroutines-test:1.9.0")

// tests that run on an emulator or phone

androidTestImplementation("androidx.compose.ui:ui-test-junit4")

Unit test of a pure function
The tip calculation from project 1 has no Android code, so it is easy to test. A good test has a clear name, a setup, an action and a check.
**`app/src/test/java/com/example/tipcalc/TipMathTest.kt`**
Testing a ViewModel with coroutines

ViewModels use `viewModelScope`, which runs on the main dispatcher, and unit tests have no main thread. The fix is a small JUnit rule that swaps the main dispatcher for a test dispatcher, so coroutines run instantly and in order.
**`app/src/test/java/com/example/todo/MainDispatcherRule.kt`**

package com.example.todo

import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers
import kotlinx.coroutines.ExperimentalCoroutinesApi
import kotlinx.coroutines.test.TestDispatcher
import kotlinx.coroutines.test.UnconfinedTestDispatcher
import kotlinx.coroutines.test.resetMain
import kotlinx.coroutines.test.setMain
import org.junit.rules.TestWatcher
import org.junit.runner.Description

// ViewModels use Dispatchers.Main, which does not exist in plain unit tests. This rule swaps in a test one.
@OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class)
class MainDispatcherRule(private val dispatcher: TestDispatcher = UnconfinedTestDispatcher()) : TestWatcher() {
    override fun starting(description: Description) = Dispatchers.setMain(dispatcher)
    override fun finished(description: Description) = Dispatchers.resetMain()
}
**`app/src/test/java/com/example/todo/TodoViewModelTest.kt`**
Testing a Compose screen
A Compose test finds elements on the screen by text or tag, performs actions and checks the results. It runs on a device or emulator.

Run local tests with the green arrow next to the test class, or with `./gradlew test`. Run instrumented tests with `./gradlew connectedAndroidTest` while an emulator is open. Every test should pass before you ship.

Performance habits

items: **Never block the main thread.** Network, database and file work belong in coroutines. Room and Retrofit suspend functions are already safe.
**Use LazyColumn with keys** for long lists, and keep each row cheap.
**Do not do heavy work inside a composable.** It can run many times. Use `remember` for expensive values and move real work to the ViewModel.
**Pass stable, small data** to composables. Passing a new list on every pass makes Compose redraw more than needed.
**Load images at the size you show them.** Coil does this for you.
**Measure, do not guess.** Android Studio's Profiler shows CPU, memory and network use. Layout Inspector shows how often composables recompose.

content.text: Crash prevention

items: Handle every network and database error with a visible state.
Use null safety and avoid `!!`.
Test with airplane mode, rotation, dark mode and a large font setting.
Use Logcat to read crash traces. The first line that names your own package usually points at the cause.
Once the app is live, use Android vitals in Play Console, or a crash reporting tool, to find crashes on real devices.

ViewModel tests check state changes with a test dispatcher.

When all pass, you can release with more confidence.

faqs.a: Cover the rules that would hurt if they broke: calculations, money, validation and state changes. Do not chase 100 percent coverage on trivial code.

lessons.title: Release Your Android App: Signing, Play Store and Interviews
lessons.metaTitle: Release Android Apps and Interview Prep
lessons.description: Prepare an Android app for release: signing, R8 shrinking, building an AAB, Google Play Console steps and common Android interview questions.

content.text: An app is only useful when real people can install it. This lesson shows how a project becomes a release on the Google Play Store, then how to talk about your work in interviews. Steps in Play Console change from time to time, so follow the current on-screen instructions if they differ.
Before you release

items: Choose a unique **application ID**, such as `com.yourname.recipes`. It cannot be changed after publishing.
Set `versionCode` (an integer that must go up with every upload) and `versionName` (the text users see).
Replace the default launcher icon with your own.
Remove test code and logging of private data.
Test on at least one real phone and one small and one large emulator.

content.text: Signing and shrinking

Android requires every app to be signed with a key that proves it comes from you. Keep this key file and its passwords safe and backed up, and never commit them to a public repository. Google Play can manage the final signing key for you (Play App Signing), and you upload with an upload key. A minimised release build uses **R8**, which removes unused code, shortens names and makes the app smaller and faster.
**`app/build.gradle.kts (release settings)`**

items: In Android Studio choose **Build > Generate Signed App Bundle or APK**.
Choose **Android App Bundle (AAB)**. Google Play requires this format for new apps.
Create a new keystore, or choose an existing one. Fill in the passwords and alias and save the file somewhere safe.
Choose the **release** build type and finish. Android Studio produces a `.aab` file.
Install the release build on a phone (for example with `bundletool`, or by uploading to internal testing) and check that nothing broke after shrinking.

content.text: If a release build crashes but the debug build does not, R8 may have removed or renamed something that is used through reflection. Add a keep rule for that class in `proguard-rules.pro`. Libraries such as Retrofit with kotlinx serialization usually ship their own rules.
Publish on Google Play

items: Create a Google Play developer account. A one-time registration fee applies, and new personal accounts may need to complete testing requirements before a production release. Check the current rules in Play Console.
Create the app in Play Console and fill in the store listing: name, short and full description, screenshots, and an icon.
Complete the forms: privacy policy (required if you handle user data), data safety, content rating and target audience.
Upload the AAB to **Internal testing** first, then to Closed or Open testing, and fix what testers find.
When ready, create a **Production** release and send it for review. Reviews can take days.
After release, read reviews and Android vitals, then ship updates with a higher `versionCode`.

content.text: Where to go next

items: **Architecture**: read Google's guide to app architecture, then practise on your own apps.
**Kotlin Flow and coroutines in depth**: testing, cancellation and error handling.
**Compose animation and custom layouts.**
**Modules, CI/CD and Gradle convention plugins** for larger teams.
**Kotlin Multiplatform**, to share logic with iOS.

content.text: Interview preparation
Interviewers want to know that you understand the basics and can explain your choices. Practise answering these aloud, using your own projects as examples.

faqs.q: APK or AAB?
faqs.a: Upload an AAB (Android App Bundle) to Google Play. Play then builds the smaller APKs each phone needs. An APK is still useful for installing directly on your own phone.

faqs.q: What if I lose my signing key?
faqs.a: With Play App Signing, Google holds the app signing key and you can ask to reset your upload key. Without it, you cannot update the app. Back up your keys safely.

faqs.q: How do I get my first Android job?
faqs.a: Publish a few real projects on GitHub, make one polished app, practise the interview questions above, and apply for junior and internship roles while you keep building.
